section.title: The House of Benjamin and Saul
section.sectionRationale: This chapter completes the Chronicler's long genealogical introduction by returning to the tribe of Benjamin in detail, tracing its families all the way down to Saul's own household. For the Chronicler's first audience, the returned exiles, Benjamin was no obscure footnote: it was, with Judah, one of the two tribes that actually resettled the land and rebuilt Jerusalem, so this list roots that audience in a family line that runs both to a king who failed and, through their own continuing place among God's people, into the ongoing story of hope.
section.thesis: Benjamin's family tree, patiently traced down to Saul's own household, quietly prepares the reader for the tragedy of chapters 9 and 10: this is the line of the king who failed, yet Benjamin's continuing presence among the resettled remnant shows that God does not discard a tribe for its king's sin, but keeps a place for it in the ongoing story that runs to David and, at last, to Christ.
section.frameNote: Seven family groups: the sons of Benjamin; Ehud's descendants and the exile to Manahath; Shaharaim's Moabite-born sons; the sons of Elpaal; the families of Shimei and Shashak; the heads of families who settled in Jerusalem and Gibeon; and, climactically, the genealogy of Saul himself, down to the skilled archers of Ulam's line.

verses.text: Benjamin was the father of Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, Aharah the third,
Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth.
The sons of Bela: Addar, Gera, Abihud,
Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah,
Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram.

units.label: Ehud's descendants and the exile to Manahath
units.note: a family already scattered before Israel's exile

verses.text: These were the descendants of Ehud who were the heads of the families living in Geba and were exiled to Manahath:
Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera, who carried them into exile and who was the father of Uzza and Ahihud.
Shaharaim had sons in the country of Moab after he had divorced his wives Hushim and Baara.
His sons by his wife Hodesh: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam,
Jeuz, Sachia, and Mirmah. These were his sons, heads of families.
He also had sons by Hushim: Abitub and Elpaal.
The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham, Shemed (who built Ono and Lod with its villages),
and Beriah and Shema (who were the heads of families living in Aijalon and who drove out the inhabitants of Gath).
Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth,
Zebadiah, Arad, Eder,
Michael, Ishpah, and Joha were the sons of Beriah.
Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber,
Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab were the sons of Elpaal.

units.label: The families of Shimei and Shashak

verses.text: Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi,
Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel,
Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath were the sons of Shimei.
Ishpan, Eber, Eliel,
Abdon, Zichri, Hanan,
Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah,
Iphdeiah, and Penuel were the sons of Shashak.
Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah,
Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri were the sons of Jeroham.

units.label: Heads of families in Jerusalem and Gibeon

verses.text: All these were heads of families, the chiefs according to their {{yachas|genealogies}}, and they lived in Jerusalem.
Jeiel the father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon. His wife's name was Maacah,
and Abdon was his firstborn son, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab,
Gedor, Ahio, Zecher,
and Mikloth, who was the father of Shimeah. They too lived alongside their relatives in Jerusalem.

units.label: Saul's genealogy
units.note: the family of the king who failed

verses.text: Ner was the father of Kish, Kish was the father of Saul, and Saul was the father of Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and {{baal|Esh-baal}}.
The son of Jonathan: {{baal|Merib-baal}}, and Merib-baal was the father of Micah.
The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz.
Ahaz was the father of Jehoaddah, Jehoaddah was the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri, and Zimri was the father of Moza.
Moza was the father of Binea. Raphah was his son, Eleasah his son, and Azel his son.
Azel had six sons, and these were their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel.
The sons of his brother Eshek: Ulam was his firstborn, Jeush second, and Eliphelet third.
The sons of Ulam were {{gibbor|mighty men of valor}}, archers, and they had many sons and grandsons, 150 in all. All these were the descendants of Benjamin.

yachas.gloss: To enroll or reckon by genealogy; a genealogical registration or pedigree. The Chronicler uses this word repeatedly across chapters 1 to 9 to describe how families were recorded, underlining that Israel's identity after the exile rested on knowing whose family, and whose promise, they belonged to.

baal.gloss: Lord, master, owner, husband; also the proper name of the Canaanite storm god. Saul's household used this word in names like Esh-baal, man of the lord, and Merib-baal, the lord contends. Later Scripture, in 2 Samuel, replaces it with bosheth, shame, showing how thoroughly Baal worship had disgraced the word by the time of the monarchy's fall.

gibbor.gloss: Mighty, a mighty man, a warrior of valor. The word marks out Benjamin's fighting reputation here, in Ulam's skilled archers, and will reappear for David's own mighty men in chapter 11, quietly measuring every human gibbor against the one true and unfailing King.

basic.context: This chapter finishes the long run of genealogies that open 1 Chronicles by circling back to Benjamin, the tribe already introduced briefly in chapter 7, and tracing it in far greater detail, all the way down to Saul, Israel's first king. It lists Benjamin's founding sons, several branching family lines, some who were exiled even before the nation's later exile, others born in Moab, families who settled Jerusalem and Gibeon, and finally Saul's own household, ending in the skilled archers descended from Ulam. The chapter answers a quiet but important question for the Chronicler's first readers: who were we before the exile, and who are we now that some of us have returned?
basic.hermeneutics: This is genealogy, not narrative, so its message comes through selection, sequence, and placement rather than plot. The Chronicler is not merely filling in names; he is deliberately setting Saul's family at the very end of Benjamin's list, right before he turns, in chapters 9 and 10, to the account of Saul's death. Reading it well means asking why this list is here at all, and the answer is that it prepares the ground for the tragedy to come while also anchoring Benjamin's ongoing identity among God's people.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter is stitched together by the language of {{yachas|genealogy}}, of families reckoned and recorded so a scattered people could know who they were. Saul's own family carries the word {{baal|baal}}, lord or master, in names like Esh-baal and Merib-baal, a word that later Scripture will not repeat once it becomes tied to Canaanite idolatry. And Benjamin's fighting reputation surfaces in the {{gibbor|mighty men}} of Ulam's line, a word that will return, transformed, around David.
basic.typology: Saul's genealogy, traced out in careful, almost affectionate detail, only to collapse in the next two chapters, stands as a shadow-picture of every merely human kingship: full of promise on paper, yet unable to endure. It throws into relief the genealogy of Judah already given in chapters 2 to 4, the line that runs to David and, at last, to Christ, the King whose house does not end in tragedy.
basic.christ: This chapter does not mention Christ directly, but it does its quiet work of contrast. Judah's genealogy has already been given at length; now Benjamin's genealogy is given at length too, ending in the king who will fail. The reader is meant to feel the difference: one line ends in disaster, the other, already marked out, will end in the everlasting throne of David's greater Son, Jesus, the King who never fails and whose kingdom cannot be shaken.
basic.god: God is the quiet keeper of every family here, none of them famous, most of them never mentioned again, yet each one recorded. He does not erase Benjamin for producing a failed king; He keeps this tribe within the story, so that generations later its descendants would stand alongside Judah among the remnant that returned. God's faithfulness to keep His people running through failure to fulfillment shows itself even in a list of names.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 9 introduces Saul himself as a young man of great promise. 2 Samuel 2:8 and 4:4 give the alternate names Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth, showing the later discomfort with the word baal. Ezra 1:5 and Nehemiah 11:4-9 record that it was Judah and Benjamin together who resettled Jerusalem after the exile, the direct fulfillment of what this chapter's placement anticipates.
basic.oneStory: Benjamin's family tree, patiently traced to its tragic end in Saul, sets up the drama of the chapters that follow, while also rooting the Chronicler's own post-exilic readers, drawn from Judah and Benjamin alike, in a story bigger than one king's failure. The line that truly endures is not Saul's but David's, already recorded earlier, and it runs at last to Jesus Christ, the King whose house will never fall.

context.literary:
This chapter is built as a funnel. It opens wide with Benjamin's five founding sons, verses 1-2, then follows several branching family lines, Ehud's household already exiled to Manahath before Israel's own exile, verse 6, Shaharaim's Moabite born sons, verse 8, Elpaal's builders and warriors, verses 12 to 18, before finally narrowing, in its last eight verses, to a single household, Saul's, traced nine generations past his own death down to the six sons of Azel and the many sonned line of Ulam. No other family in the entire chapter receives anything close to that depth of continued tracing after its most famous member dies; the text spends more verses on Saul's descendants than on Saul himself, an imbalance that only makes sense as deliberate preparation for what chapters 9 and 10 are about to narrate.

The chapter also repeats itself on purpose. Several names, Ahio, Zichri, Elpaal's household generally, recur across different family groupings, and Jeiel's Gibeon household, verses 29-32, will be repeated nearly verbatim at 9:35-38, a doubling the Chronicler uses elsewhere, most notably for Levi in chapter 6, whenever he wants a genealogy to serve two purposes at once, here bridging Benjamin's tribal record directly into the narrative resumption at 9:35, where Saul's genealogy appears again immediately before his death is finally told.
context.historical:
Benjamin occupied a narrow strip of hill country between Ephraim and Judah, small in territory yet strategically decisive, since it held both Gibeah, Saul's own hometown, and Jerusalem itself before David's conquest made the city Judah's in practice. The towns named across this chapter, Geba, Aijalon, Lod, Ono, Gibeon, Jerusalem, sit almost entirely within or beside that narrow strip, confirming that this genealogy, however sprawling its names, describes a genuinely compact and well known territory rather than a scattered diaspora.

Verse 6's note that Ehud's descendants "were exiled to Manahath" records a deportation that predates Israel's national exile altogether, most likely tied to earlier regional conflict rather than to Assyria or Babylon, a reminder that displacement was not a single catastrophic event in Israel's history but a recurring feature of tribal life even in settled times. Verse 8's report that Shaharaim fathered sons "in the country of Moab after he had divorced his wives" places one branch of Benjamin's family temporarily outside the land entirely, a small, otherwise unremarked detail that shows Israelite family lines crossing national borders casually, well before exile made such crossing a matter of national trauma.

By the time this chapter's final names were being recorded, Benjamin's chief historical distinction, alongside Judah, was having actually resettled Jerusalem after Babylon; Ezra 2:1 and Nehemiah 11:4-9 list precisely the two tribes this genealogical prologue treats at greatest length.
context.canonical:
Benjamin's birth itself already carried a tension this chapter's ending will resolve into tragedy: his dying mother named him Ben-oni, son of my sorrow, while his father renamed him Benjamin, son of the right hand, Genesis 35:16-18, sorrow and strength named over the very same child within one verse. Centuries of Benjaminite history run along both those tracks at once, the tribe supplies Israel's first king, real strength, and also the near destruction of Judges 20 and now Saul's own downfall, real sorrow, so that this chapter's genealogy sits inside a much older pattern already set at the tribe's very naming.

The chapter's placement anticipates 1 Chronicles 9:35-44, which repeats this same Saul genealogy almost word for word immediately before narrating his death in chapter 10, a doubling that frames Saul's story with his own family on both sides, once as introduction and once as immediate prelude to the battle of Gilboa. Later Scripture keeps returning to this tribe on both registers: Hosea 5:8-9 summons Benjamin to a coming battle centuries after Saul, and Paul, "of the tribe of Benjamin," Philippians 3:5, becomes proof that God's purposes for this tribe did not end with its king's failure, running instead all the way to an apostle who calls his own earlier confidence in that lineage rubbish compared to knowing Christ, Philippians 3:8.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
By placing Saul's genealogy at the very end of Benjamin's family record, immediately before resuming his narrative in chapters 9 and 10, the Chronicler wants his readers to feel Saul's coming death as a family event, not merely a private, isolated failure. Every name traced after Saul, down to Ulam's 150 sons and grandsons skilled as archers, verse 40, insists that a king's downfall did not end his household, and by direct extension did not end his tribe; Benjamin continues, generation after generation, long past the disaster the very next chapters will narrate.

The author also intends the sheer density of this chapter, seven separate family groups where the previous chapter gave neighboring tribes only a few verses each, to establish Benjamin's importance to his own post-exilic audience directly, since it was Benjamin, alongside Judah, who actually resettled Jerusalem and therefore needed its own identity rooted this deeply in the record.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter offers no moral lesson stated in so many words; it is pure genealogical description, family after family, town after town, with no verse instructing the reader how to live. Its teaching arrives through placement rather than statement: readers are meant to notice that a tribe's worst chapter, producing a king who dies in disgrace, does not become its only chapter, since the same tribe's descendants are later found resettling Jerusalem and, later still, producing an apostle to the Gentiles.

Nothing here prescribes genealogical record keeping as a spiritual discipline, nor does the survival of Saul's line into detailed record suggest any special favor toward his particular descendants; the enduring principle is simply that God tracks families through failure without letting failure be the last word on them.

debates.question: Why does Chronicles preserve the baal element in names like Esh-baal and Merib-baal when 2 Samuel replaces it with bosheth, shame?

views.label: Chronicles retains the older, unedited historical form
views.case: Baal originally simply meant lord or master and, especially in Israel's earliest monarchy, could even be used of the LORD Himself, Hosea 2:16; the Chronicler, writing generations after the exile had already settled the question of Baal worship for good, had no need to euphemize the ancient family names and simply preserved the genealogical record as he received it.

views.label: Samuel's bosheth substitution reflects the shame later attached to the name
views.case: By the time these names reached their final written form in Samuel, or in the scribal tradition behind it, the word baal had become so identified with Canaanite idolatry that pious scribes substituted bosheth wherever it appeared in personal names, both to avoid honoring a false god in speech and to mark the disgrace idolatry had brought on Saul's house.

debates.bearing: Either way, the underlying reality does not change: Saul's household bore names built on a word that could mean lord generically or the Canaanite god specifically, and the son who carried one of them, Merib-baal, later received remarkable, unearned kindness from David, 2 Samuel 9, a small foretaste of the mercy that reaches into every compromised and disgraced house through Christ.

debates.question: Why record Benjamin's genealogy in such detail right before narrating Saul's downfall?

views.label: To prepare a stark contrast with David's already-established line
views.case: Chapters 2 to 4 have already traced Judah's genealogy in detail, culminating in David; placing Benjamin's genealogy, ending in Saul, immediately before the account of his death in chapters 9 and 10 invites the reader to feel the difference between the king who failed and the king God had already chosen, whose line the Chronicler treasures far more.

views.label: To honor Benjamin's ongoing place in the covenant community
views.case: The Chronicler is not interested only in condemning Saul; he takes real care to record Benjamin's families in full, showing that this tribe, despite producing a failed king, remains a full and valued part of Israel, a tribe that, alongside Judah, will physically resettle Jerusalem, 1 Chronicles 9:3.

debates.bearing: Both readings work together: the genealogy soberly prepares the reader for Saul's tragic end while also affirming that a tribe's, or a family's, worst chapter does not define its entire future in God's purposes.

study.originalLanguages:
Yachas, the verb behind "genealogies" in verse 28, describes formal enrollment or reckoning into an official record, not mere memory or reputation; the Chronicler uses this same word across chapters 1 to 9 whenever he wants readers to understand that a name's presence here is the result of verified registration, not casual inclusion, which matters enormously for a chapter about to record, in careful fashion, exactly which family produced Israel's failed first king.

Baal, lord or master, sits inside Esh-baal, man of the lord, and Merib-baal, the lord contends, verses 33-34, a title that in Israel's earliest monarchy could still be used innocently of the LORD Himself; Hosea 2:16 records God saying His people will one day call Him "my Husband" and no longer "my Master," the very word translated Master there being this same baal, before Canaanite worship made the word too dangerous to keep. Later scribes replace it with bosheth, shame, in 2 Samuel's parallel names, Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth, a substitution so deliberate that it marks the very moment Israel's ordinary vocabulary had curdled into embarrassment.

Gibbor, mighty, describes Ulam's archer sons in the chapter's final verse, the same word Chronicles will use again for David's own elite soldiers in chapter 11, so that a reader who has just finished Benjamin's genealogy meets, almost immediately afterward, a different company of mighty men gathering not around Saul's house but around David's, the word itself outliving the king who first commanded warriors bearing it.

And Benjamin's own name preserves a small drama the genealogy never restates. Yamin, right hand, the source of the tribe's name, was his father's word of strength spoken over a son his dying mother had already named Ben-oni, son of my sorrow, Genesis 35:18; every genealogy of this tribe, this one included, is technically a genealogy of the son of the right hand, strength deliberately spoken over a birth that had just cost a mother her life, sorrow and strength bound together in one child's name from his very first breath.

That double naming is not incidental to this chapter's own structure. A tribe named for both sorrow and strength at once produces, in the very same genealogy, a king who ends in disgrace and a company of skilled archers still called mighty at the chapter's close, as though the two halves of Benjamin's ancient name kept quietly reasserting themselves in every generation the Chronicler had records for.

typology.type: Saul's genealogy, carefully traced yet ending in collapse
typology.fulfillment: Nine generations of Saul's descendants are recorded here with the same careful attention given to any other family, yet the office that made Saul worth recording in the first place, kingship, never survives him; every later name in his line is a private person, not a ruler. Luke 1:32-33 promises the opposite outcome for David's greater Son, the Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, His kingdom will never end, a throne this chapter's own careful record of failure throws into sharper relief by contrast.

typology.type: Benjamin's continued place among the resettled remnant
typology.fulfillment: A tribe whose most famous son died in disgrace on Mount Gilboa, 1 Samuel 31:1-6, nonetheless supplies half the community that later rebuilds Jerusalem, Nehemiah 11:4-9, and eventually an apostle who calls his own Benjaminite pedigree rubbish next to knowing Christ, Philippians 3:5-8. Ephesians 2:14-16 states the wider pattern this anticipates, Christ has made the two one and is reconciling both of them to God in one body, Judah and Benjamin, and every dividing history besides, drawn together in Him.

typology.type: Merib-baal, grandson of the failed king, welcomed permanently at David's table
typology.fulfillment: David's kindness in 2 Samuel 9 reaches a young man from the very house that had hunted him, lame, dependent, carrying a name still marked by the shame later scribes attached to baal, and seats him permanently among the king's own sons. Romans 5:8 describes the pattern in full, God demonstrates His own love for us in this, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, grace reaching, as it did for Merib-baal, not toward the deserving but toward the disgraced, seated at a table the disgraced could never have earned their own way to.

study.christ:
This chapter never names Christ, yet its very last movement, tracing Saul's family nine generations deep only to arrive at private names with no further kingship attached, Azel's six sons, Ulam's skilled archers, does its work by absence. Judah's royal line, already recorded at length in chapters 2 to 4 and running to David, is the line Chronicles clearly treasures; Benjamin's, however carefully preserved, simply stops mattering politically the moment Saul dies. Luke 1:32-33 supplies the reason that contrast exists at all: David's greater Son receives "the throne of His father David" and "will reign over the house of Jacob forever," a permanence Saul's whole meticulously documented household never comes close to matching.

Merib-baal supplies Christ by grace rather than by throne. Crippled, hidden away, carrying in his very name the shame later scribes would formalize as bosheth, he is the last person David's own political interest would require him to seek out, yet 2 Samuel 9:7 has David say exactly the opposite of what self interest demands, "I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan," restoring land and a permanent seat "at my table" to a member of the house that had hunted David for years. That kindness, extended from the true king's line to the failed king's own grandson, previews the shape of the gospel precisely, mercy that does not wait for the disgraced to earn their way back but goes looking for them, Luke 19:10, "the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost."

The tension in Benjamin's own name, Ben-oni, son of sorrow, renamed Benjamin, son of the right hand, Genesis 35:18, plays out across this whole chapter and the two that follow: sorrow in Saul's coming death, strength in the tribe's ongoing survival and eventual resettlement of Jerusalem. Both halves of that ancient naming find their fullest resolution in Christ, who is Himself well acquainted with sorrow, Isaiah 53:3, and yet is seated, Hebrews 1:3, at the right hand of the Majesty on high, strength and sorrow no longer in tension in Him but perfectly, permanently reconciled, exactly as they had been spoken, in miniature, over one dying mother's final child.
study.god:
God is shown here as the quiet keeper of every family this chapter names, none of them famous, most never mentioned again in Scripture, yet every one recorded with the same careful attention given to Saul's own household. He does not withdraw His record keeping from a tribe because its most visible son failed; the seven family groups traced here receive, if anything, more space than any neighboring tribe in the previous chapter, a deliberate abundance rather than a diminished one.

He is patient with compromised worship in a way that still, eventually, corrects itself. Names built on baal persist in this chapter without comment, yet the same broader record shows later scribes replacing that title with bosheth once its associations became unbearable, a small, internal witness to a community gradually recognizing and repairing its own inherited compromises rather than either excusing them forever or erasing the evidence that they ever existed.

He is faithful to a covenant kindness that outlasts political failure. Nothing in this chapter states it directly, yet the record of Merib-baal, grandson of the very king this chapter has just finished tracing, sets up 2 Samuel 9's account of David's kindness "for the sake of your father Jonathan," God's own faithfulness to covenant friendship working itself out through one king's mercy toward a rival's crippled grandson, long after any political reason for that mercy had disappeared.

And He is sovereign over which tribe's line receives an unending throne without thereby discarding the tribes that do not. Benjamin produces the first king and loses the office forever within one generation; Judah, already recorded at length earlier in this book, receives the everlasting promise instead, yet Benjamin is not therefore cut off, remaining paired with Judah at the return from exile and later producing the apostle to the Gentiles, evidence that God's larger purposes distribute differently across His people's tribes without any tribe becoming worthless once it stops holding the throne. The God of this chapter measures a family's value by something other than the office its most famous member once held.

crossReferences.note: Saul is introduced as an impressive young man, a head taller than any of the people, every outward mark of a king Israel could be proud of. The genealogy recorded here, ending nine generations later in ordinary, unremarkable names, quietly measures how much of that early promise actually endured within his own household.

Esh-baal becomes Ish-bosheth in Samuel's later narrative, the word baal, lord, replaced by bosheth, shame, once Canaanite associations made the original title too costly to keep speaking aloud. Chronicles preserves the older, unedited form, letting a careful reader watch the very moment Israel's vocabulary caught up with its theology.

David's search for anyone left of the house of Saul to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan's sake lands on Merib-baal, crippled and living in obscurity, and ends with him eating permanently at the king's table like one of the king's own sons. The genealogy traced here in verses 33-34 is the very family line that kindness reaches into.

The returning exiles who resettle Jerusalem are counted by family precisely as this chapter counts Benjamin, and Nehemiah names Benjaminite households living in the city in language that echoes verse 28's own report of Benjaminite chiefs who lived in Jerusalem. The tribe traced here in judgment's shadow is the same tribe found, generations later, rebuilding the very city.

Rachel names her dying son Ben-oni, son of my sorrow, while Jacob renames him Benjamin, son of the right hand, sorrow and strength spoken over the same child within one verse. Every genealogy of this tribe, this chapter included, carries both names at once, Saul's disgrace answering to the sorrow, the tribe's ongoing survival answering to the strength.

Benjamin's 700 elite left handed slingers, each of whom could sling a stone at a hair without missing, fought in the civil war that nearly ended the tribe altogether generations before Saul. Ulam's own skilled archers in this chapter's final verse continue a martial reputation this small tribe had already earned, and nearly lost everything defending, long before its most famous son ever took the throne.

Saul dies alongside three of his own sons named earlier in this very chapter, Jonathan, Malchishua, and Abinadab, verse 33, on the same day, a single battle erasing in an afternoon what this genealogy took nine generations to record on his behalf. The list that seemed so secure on the page proves, within a single chapter's turn, how fragile any merely human throne actually is.

Paul lists his own credentials, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, the same tribe this chapter traces at such length, before calling every one of those credentials rubbish compared to knowing Christ, Philippians 3:8. The tribe that produced a failed king also, centuries later, produced a man who found his true identity entirely outside his tribal pedigree.

Hosea summons Benjamin to battle centuries after Saul, lead on, O Benjamin, proof that the tribe remained a recognized, active part of Israel's story long after this chapter's genealogy was first written down, still being addressed by name, still expected to answer when the prophets called.

study.oneStory:
Benjamin enters Scripture already carrying two names at once, Ben-oni, son of sorrow, spoken by a dying mother, and Benjamin, son of the right hand, spoken by a grieving father over the very same child, Genesis 35:16-18. This chapter's long, careful genealogy, ending in Saul's household nine generations deep, is the sorrow half of that naming finally working itself out in full: a king who looked like Israel's proudest hope dies in a single battle, and the record here spends more space on his descendants after his fall than the whole nation spent celebrating him before it.

Yet the same tribe carries the other half of its name into the rest of the story. The Benjamin traced here in the shadow of a coming defeat is the same Benjamin that, alongside Judah, actually walks back into Jerusalem generations later to rebuild it, Ezra and Nehemiah both naming these returning families in terms that echo this very chapter's own language of households and settlements. Strength did not vanish from this tribe when its king fell; it simply waited, through exile and return, for another occasion.

The furthest reach of that waiting is Paul, a Benjaminite by pedigree who counts that pedigree rubbish next to knowing Christ, the same move this whole chapter has been quietly making by placing Saul's failure inside a genealogy that keeps going regardless. What began as sorrow at one birth, deepened into national tragedy at one death, and matured into new identity in one apostle traces, across centuries, the same pattern the whole Bible tells at a larger scale: real loss, honestly recorded rather than hidden, answered not by erasing the sorrowful name but by placing a stronger one permanently beside it, until the two are no longer in tension at all in the Son who sits, sorrow and strength reconciled, at the right hand of the Father Himself.

quiz.q: Why does the Chronicler pause to give Benjamin's genealogy again here, at greater length than in chapter 7?

options.text: To trace the line down to Saul's own household, setting up the tragic account of his death in chapters 9 and 10.
options.note: The chapter's placement, right before Saul's death is narrated, is deliberate literary preparation.

options.text: Because Benjamin was a large and important tribe worth recording in full.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it misses the specific link this list forges to Saul's coming downfall.

options.text: Because the Chronicler had simply run out of new material to record.
options.note: A dismissive half-truth; the Chronicler is working with clear purpose, not filler.

options.text: Because Benjamin was about to be permanently excluded from Israel.
options.note: False; Benjamin remains part of Israel and later resettles Jerusalem alongside Judah.

quiz.q: What do names like Esh-baal and Merib-baal preserve, and how do they differ from their forms in 2 Samuel?

options.text: The original names built on baal, lord or master; 2 Samuel later substitutes bosheth, shame, reflecting how Baal worship had disgraced that title.
options.note: Verses 33-34 compared with 2 Samuel 2:8 and 4:4 show exactly this substitution.

options.text: Ordinary family names that simply reflected that generation's culture.
options.note: Partly true, but it misses the theological weight of the later name change.

options.text: Names Saul deliberately chose to honor the Canaanite god Baal.
options.note: Overstates the case; baal could simply mean lord, and deliberate idol-worship in the naming is not stated in the text.

options.text: Names invented by the Chronicler with no historical basis.
options.note: False; the names are part of the received genealogical tradition, confirmed across both Samuel and Chronicles.

quiz.q: Where does Benjamin fit into the story of the returned exiles, the Chronicler's first audience?

options.text: Benjamin, alongside Judah, was one of the two tribes that actually resettled Jerusalem after the exile, so this genealogy roots the Chronicler's own audience in the story.
options.note: Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 11 confirm Judah and Benjamin as the returning core of the community.

options.text: Benjamin remained part of Israel's story even after Saul's failure.
options.note: True, but vague; it misses the specific historical detail of the return from exile.

options.text: Benjamin merged entirely into Judah and lost its own tribal identity.
options.note: A half-truth; Benjamin was closely allied with Judah but is still named separately in the records of the return.

options.text: Benjamin was cut off from Israel entirely because of Saul's sin.
options.note: False; the text and later history show Benjamin continuing as a recognized tribe.

quiz.q: What is the literary effect of ending this chapter with Saul's genealogy right before chapters 9 and 10?

options.text: It sets the stage for the fall of Saul, contrasting his tragic line with the enduring line of David already traced in earlier chapters.
options.note: The Chronicler builds a deliberate contrast between Judah's line, chapters 2-4, and Benjamin's, ending here in tragedy.

options.text: It simply shows that Saul had many descendants.
options.note: True as a bare fact, but it misses the contrastive, preparatory purpose of the placement.

options.text: It proves that Saul's family continued to reign as kings after him.
options.note: Misleading; Saul's dynasty as king ended with him, even though his family line continued.

options.text: It has no connection to the chapters that follow.
options.note: False; the very next chapters narrate Saul's genealogy again and then his death.

quiz.q: How does this genealogy point forward to Christ?

options.text: By setting up the contrast between Saul's failed kingship and the everlasting line of David, which finds its fulfillment in Jesus, the true and unfailing King.
options.note: The chapter's placement makes the reader feel the difference between a house that fails and a house that endures forever in Christ.

options.text: By showing God's care in remembering every family, a pattern of grace fulfilled in Christ's care for His people.
options.note: True and fitting, but more generic; it misses the specific Saul-versus-David contrast the chapter is building.

options.text: By showing that a king from any tribe would have served Israel equally well.
options.note: Misplaces the emphasis; the text is building toward one particular chosen line, Judah's, not treating all tribes as equal candidates for kingship.

options.text: By showing that genealogies have no bearing on the gospel story.
options.note: False; the genealogies of Chronicles are foundational to tracing the promised line that leads to Christ.

questions: Benjamin's genealogy quietly sets up Saul's tragic fall two chapters later. Where in your own life have you seen God preparing you for a hard lesson before you even knew it was coming?

Even the tribe of the failed king, Benjamin, found its place again among the resettled remnant after the exile. How does that shape the way you think about your own past failures and God's willingness to keep you in His story?

The names Esh-baal and Merib-baal remind us how easily God's people can absorb the language and values of the cultures around them. Where might you be unconsciously borrowing the world's names for what only God should be called?
This long list of ordinary, largely forgotten names still mattered enough for God to record. What does that tell you about how God sees the details of your own life and family?
Saul's line ends in tragedy, but David's line, already traced earlier in Chronicles, endures forever in Christ. Whose house are you building your hope on today?

translationNotes.note: BSB footnotes explain that Esh-baal is also called Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel 2:8, and Merib-baal is called Mephibosheth in 2 Samuel 4:4; the change from baal, lord, to bosheth, shame, reflects later discomfort with the word baal.
Some Septuagint manuscripts read the father of Gibeon where the Hebrew reads simply Gibeon, understood as the founder of the town; compare 1 Chronicles 9:35.

The sons of Ulam are noted as skilled archers among mighty men of valor, a martial reputation within Benjamin that echoes the tribe's skilled left-handed warriors elsewhere in Scripture, such as Judges 20:16.
